title: Wavelength-controlled photothermal reduction of carbon dioxide to produce fuels over Nb 2 AlC/TiO 2  heterostructures in a continuous-flow reactor
content: A highly conductive Nb2AlC MAX phase was coupled with TiO2 to construct Nb2AlC/TiO2 heterostructures and evaluated for CO2 photothermal reduction under solar radiations. Incorporation of 10 wt% Nb2AlC into TiO2 significantly improved the photocatalytic performance with 858.8 and 10.5 µmol g−1 h−1 of CO and H2 respectively with a water–methanol mixture at 150 °C. Using the water–methanol mixture, the CO production rate is 77.7 and 1.7 fold higher than using water and pristine TiO2 only. Similarly, the corresponding rates were 3.6 and 1.2 fold higher for H2 production. The enhanced photocatalytic activity is attributed to the synergistic interaction between Nb2AlC and TiO2 which facilitates efficient separation and transfer of charge carriers. The effect of reaction temperature on the distribution of reduction products was investigated in detail. In situ DRIFT analysis revealed changes in the interactions of CO2 with the catalyst surface at different temperatures and also the intermediate species involved during the photocatalytic reaction. Changes in the CO/H2 ratio with increasing temperature indicate that the syngas composition can be effectively regulated by adjusting the reaction temperature over the Nb2AlC/TiO2 heterostructure. Control experiments under dark conditions at 150 °C produced no detectable products confirming the photo-assisted process rather than thermal conversion. The temperature and irradiation-dependent product distribution demonstrates the potential of Nb2AlC/TiO2 for controllable CO2 conversion under continuous-flow conditions. The material also showed consistent performance throughout five consecutive reuse experiments, with no meaningful decline in product generation. These observations support the use of Nb2AlC/TiO2 heterostructures for light assisted CO2 conversion and for producing syngas with an adjustable CO to H2 ratio. These findings highlight the use of a conductive Nb2AlC MAX phase as a promising noble-metal-free co-catalyst strategy for thermally assisted CO2 conversion.
